newsitem.title: Switzerland: FOCUS-Bundesbank, Bonn close to revaluation deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank, Bonn close to revaluation deal.

text.p: The Bundesbank and the German government are close to sealing a deal on revaluing some of the assets of the independent central bank, but this will not lead to any additional money being handed over to Bonn in 1997, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said.
"There is no formal agreement, but we are relatively close," Tietmeyer told reporters late on Tuesday during a dinner at the International Monetary Conference (IMC).

Details of the deal are sketchy, but Tietmeyer stressed that the talks did not focus on a revaluation of Germany's gold, an issue that has raised concern about measures to meet the Maastricht criteria and the credibility of Europe's single currency.
"In 1998 we will look at whether there are some elements that can be revalued, but this is not about the issue of gold," Tietmeyer said, adding:
"We are not talking about gold" and "in 1997 there is no money," Tietmeyer said, referring to the talks.

Tietmeyer's comments seem to confirm statements earlier today by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel who said he and Tietmeyer had reached "a good compromise" on his controversial plan to revalue gold and currency reserves.

Waigel gave no details of the compromise but other top officials said Bonn had accepted a plan which effectively blocked it from benefiting this year from the asset revaluation process -- bad news for a state struggling to rein in its deficit amid record unemployment levels.

Hermann Otto Solms, parliamentary leader of the junior coalition partner, the Free Democrats (FDP), said Bonn had agreed to accept the Bundesbank's offer to delay any transfer of funds until 1998, although the revaluation itself would in fact take place in 1997.
Waigel conceded that the deal with Tietmeyer had to be approved by a central bank committee.

Waigel's gold plans had sparked an unprecedented split with Tietmeyer, who flatly rejected an initial proposal which envisaged a transfer to Bonn from the revaluation this year, thus aiding Germany's chance of meeting Maastricht goals.
The Bundesbank had objected in particular to the original timing for the plan, saying it endangered Germany's image as a by-the-rules player on monetary union and infringed on its own autonomy.
This year is crucial for monetary union, since participants in the planned euro launch in January 1999 will be chosen on the basis of 1997 data, in May 1998.
Germany is struggling in particular to plug its budget deficit, with the Maastricht Treaty calling for countries to limit their deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
The dispute between the Bundesbank and Bonn had sparked widespread public and political fears that Germany was resorting to creative accounting for the euro, and triggered calls for Waigel to resign.

Deputies who attended a closed door meeting in Bonn on Tuesday said Waigel claimed he was 19 billion marks short in his 1997 budget and that Chancellor Helmut Kohl had backed him up in plans for spending cuts and more privatisations.
Waigel has said he expected to take in 10 billion marks from sales of Bonn's shares in Deutsche Telekom and another three billion from cuts in planned spending, the deputies said.
